title: React Rendering: A Field Handbook to Reconciliation, Keys & Memoization
summary: A dense, practical guide to how React decides what to re-render — the render/commit phases, the reconciliation diffing algorithm, why keys matter, and how memo, useMemo, and useCallback actually change the picture. Covers mechanics, real usage patterns, cost trade-offs, and the mistakes that make memoization useless or harmful.

chapters.title: What 'Render' Actually Means
points: Definition: a render is React calling your component function to get a description of UI — it is NOT a DOM update.
Three distinct phases: Trigger (something schedules work) → Render (call components, diff) → Commit (apply DOM mutations).
Render phase must be pure: no DOM writes, no fetches, no mutation of props/state/module variables — React may call it twice or throw it away.
Commit phase is where refs are attached and useLayoutEffect runs synchronously; useEffect runs after paint.
Component returns React elements — plain objects like {type: 'div', props: {...}, key, ref} — created by jsx()/createElement.
Elements are immutable descriptions; the Fiber node is the mutable work object React keeps across renders.
Re-render ≠ DOM change: React can render 50 components and commit zero DOM mutations.
Initial mount vs update: mount builds the whole tree, update diffs against the previous tree.
Mental model: `UI = f(state)`. React's job is computing the minimal DOM delta between f(state1) and f(state2).
In StrictMode dev, components render twice to surface impure render logic — this does not happen in production.

chapters.title: What Triggers a Re-render
points: Trigger 1: state update in the component itself — useState setter or useReducer dispatch.
Trigger 2: parent re-rendered — a child re-renders by default regardless of whether its props changed.
Trigger 3: context value the component consumes changed (by Object.is on the value).
Trigger 4: a subscribed external store changed via useSyncExternalStore.
Trigger 5: forceUpdate / key change on the element (key change is actually remount, not re-render).
Props changing is NOT itself a trigger — the parent rendering is; props are just what got passed down during that render.
Bail-out rule: `setState(sameValue)` with Object.is equality may skip the re-render, but React may still render once more before bailing out.
Updates are batched: multiple setStates in one event handler (and, since React 18, in timeouts/promises/native handlers too) produce one render.
Functional updater `setCount(c => c + 1)` is required when the next state depends on the previous inside a batch.
Setting state during render of the same component is legal (render-phase update) and React re-runs immediately without committing.
Common myth to kill: 'React re-renders only what changed' — React re-renders the subtree by default and diffs to minimize DOM work.

chapters.title: Reconciliation: The Diffing Algorithm
points: Goal: given old tree and new tree, produce the minimal set of DOM operations — the general tree-diff problem is O(n³), React heuristically does O(n).
Heuristic 1: elements of different type produce entirely different trees — React unmounts the old subtree and mounts fresh.
Heuristic 2: developers can hint stable identity across renders with the `key` prop.
Same type, same position → React keeps the DOM node and Fiber, updates only changed attributes/props.
Different type (`<div>` → `<span>`, or `<Profile>` → `<Feed>`) → old DOM destroyed, state lost, effects cleaned up, refs detached.
Position in the tree defines identity: `{cond ? <Input/> : <Input/>}` keeps state because both are `Input` at the same slot.
Children without keys are diffed by index — inserting at the front makes React think every item changed.
Component state lives on the Fiber, keyed by (type, position) — so state survives as long as type and position hold.
Fiber architecture: two trees (current + workInProgress) enable interruptible, resumable rendering; the swap at commit is a pointer flip (double buffering).
Bailout during reconciliation: if props are referentially equal and no state/context changed, React can clone the child fibers and skip re-rendering the subtree entirely.
Diffing text: string/number children are updated in place via nodeValue, cheapest possible case.

chapters.title: Keys: Identity Across Renders
points: A key tells React which item in a list is which, so it can match old and new children by identity instead of index.
Keys must be stable (same item → same key across renders), unique among siblings (not globally), and predictable (not random).
`key={Math.random()}` or `key={uuid()}` inline destroys and remounts every item on every render — worst case for performance and state.
`key={index}` is safe only for static, never-reordered, never-filtered, append-only lists with no per-item state.
Index-key bug demo: a list of `<input>`s reordered by index keeps the typed values glued to positions, not to items.
Correct: `items.map(item => <Row key={item.id} {...item} />)` — key comes from the data's stable ID.
Keys are consumed by React and NOT passed to the component — reading `props.key` inside is undefined; pass `id={item.id}` separately if needed.
Keys work on Fragments too: `<Fragment key={id}>` (the `<>` shorthand cannot take a key).
Deliberate remount trick: `<UserForm key={userId} />` resets all internal state when the user changes — cheaper and clearer than a syncing useEffect.
Deliberate preservation trick: give two different branches the SAME key/position to keep state, or different keys to force a reset.
Keys never need to be globally unique — two different lists may both use key='1'.

chapters.title: React.memo: Stopping the Cascade
points: `React.memo(Component)` returns a memoized component that skips re-rendering when its props are shallowly equal to last render's props.
Shallow equality: Object.is compared per prop key — nested objects are compared by reference, not deeply.
memo breaks the 'parent renders → child renders' chain; without it the entire subtree below a rendering parent re-renders.
Second argument: custom comparator `memo(Comp, (prev, next) => boolean)` — return true to SKIP the render (opposite polarity of shouldComponentUpdate).
memo does not stop re-renders caused by the component's own state or by a context it consumes.
One unstable prop defeats memo entirely: an inline `onClick={() => ...}`, `style={{}}`, or `data={[...]}` is a new reference every parent render.
Example of a broken memo: `<MemoRow onSelect={() => select(id)} />` — memo never hits.

Children-as-props escape hatch: `<Wrapper><Expensive /></Wrapper>` — `children` is created by the parent's parent, so its reference stays stable and Wrapper's re-render doesn't re-render Expensive. No memo needed.
memo is only worth it when the component is genuinely expensive OR renders often with the same props OR is a large subtree root.
memo on a leaf that renders a single `<span>` costs more (comparison + memory) than it saves.
React Compiler (React 19+) auto-inserts memoization, making most manual memo/useMemo/useCallback unnecessary in compiled code.

chapters.title: useMemo: Caching Values
points: Signature: `const value = useMemo(() => computeExpensive(a, b), [a, b])` — caches the RESULT between renders while deps are unchanged.
Deps compared with Object.is, element by element; any change re-runs the factory during render.
Two distinct jobs: (1) skip expensive computation, (2) preserve referential identity of an object/array so a downstream memo or dep array holds.
Referential-identity use case: `const style = useMemo(() => ({width}), [width])` passed to a memoized child.
It's a cache with one entry and no guarantee — React may discard cached values (e.g. to free memory for offscreen content), so the factory must be pure and cheap-to-redo-correctly.
Never put side effects inside useMemo — it runs during render.
Do not use useMemo for correctness; code must still work if every useMemo recomputed every render.
Measure first: wrap the computation in `console.time`/`timeEnd`, or throttle CPU 4-6× in DevTools before deciding it's 'expensive'.
Rule of thumb: if it's under ~1ms and not feeding a memo boundary, skip it.
Empty deps `[]` = compute once for the component's lifetime; missing deps array = no memoization at all (and a lint error).
useMemo caches within one component instance — remounting (or a key change) throws the cache away.

chapters.title: useCallback: Caching Functions
points: `useCallback(fn, deps)` is exactly `useMemo(() => fn, deps)` — sugar for memoizing a function reference.
Purpose is referential stability, not speed: creating a closure is cheap; the cost is the re-render it triggers downstream.
Needed when the function is (a) a prop to a memo'd child, (b) a dependency of useEffect/useMemo, or (c) passed to a custom hook that deps on it.
Useless when the consumer is a plain DOM element: `<button onClick={cb}>` gains nothing from useCallback.
Stale closure hazard: `useCallback(() => setCount(count+1), [])` captures count=0 forever — fix with the functional updater `c => c+1` to keep deps empty legitimately.
Deps must include every reactive value the function reads; the exhaustive-deps lint rule is the guard.
Chain rule: a useCallback is only stable if all of its own deps are stable — one unstable dep poisons the whole chain up the tree.
For effects, prefer moving the function INSIDE the effect over stabilizing it with useCallback.
Event-handler alternative: a ref-based 'latest callback' pattern (or the `useEffectEvent` API) gives a permanently stable handle that always reads fresh values.
Returning callbacks from a custom hook? Wrap them — consumers can't stabilize what you hand them.
Anti-pattern: blanket-wrapping every handler in useCallback 'just in case' — adds deps arrays, allocations, and lint noise for zero gain.

chapters.title: Context and Re-renders
points: Every consumer of a context re-renders when the provider's `value` changes by Object.is — memo does NOT block a context update.
Classic bug: `<Ctx.Provider value={{user, setUser}}>` creates a new object every provider render, re-rendering every consumer.
Fix: `const value = useMemo(() => ({user, setUser}), [user])`.
Split contexts by change frequency: a stable dispatch/actions context plus a volatile state context, so action-only consumers never re-render.
State-and-dispatch pattern: `<StateCtx.Provider value={state}><DispatchCtx.Provider value={dispatch}>` — dispatch from useReducer is permanently stable.
Context has no selector — you cannot subscribe to one field of the value; consumers get all-or-nothing.
Workarounds for selection: useSyncExternalStore, a subscription-based store (Zustand/Redux), or use-context-selector.
A provider re-rendering re-renders its children only through the normal parent-child rule; pass `children` through to avoid that.
Deeply nested consumers still re-render even if an intermediate memo'd component sits between them and the provider.
Trade-off: context is ideal for low-frequency values (theme, locale, auth) and poor for high-frequency ones (mouse position, form input).

chapters.title: State Colocation & Structural Fixes
points: The cheapest re-render optimization is a smaller re-render scope — move state DOWN to the smallest component that uses it.
Before: input state in the page root re-renders the whole tree on each keystroke. After: extract `<SearchInput>` owning its own state.
Lift content UP: pass expensive subtrees as `children` or as props so they're created by an outer component and skip re-creation.
Splitting a component often beats adding memo — it's zero runtime cost and no dep arrays.
Derive, don't duplicate: computing `fullName` during render is better than a state + useEffect sync (which causes an extra render pass).
Avoid `useEffect` + `setState` to mirror props — use the key-reset trick or compute during render.
Prefer useReducer when several state fields update together — one dispatch = one render instead of several setStates (though React 18 batches anyway).
Uncontrolled inputs + refs eliminate per-keystroke renders entirely for forms that only need values on submit.
List virtualization (react-window / TanStack Virtual) beats memoizing 10,000 rows — render 20 instead of memoizing 10,000.
useDeferredValue / startTransition mark an update as non-urgent, keeping typing responsive while a heavy list re-renders in the background.

chapters.title: Measuring: Prove It Before You Fix It
points: React DevTools Profiler: record an interaction, read the flamegraph — width = time, and 'why did this render?' requires enabling 'Record why each component rendered'.
The Profiler shows render reasons: props changed / state changed / hooks changed / parent rendered / context changed.
DevTools setting 'Highlight updates when components render' gives a live visual of the cascade.
`<Profiler id onRender={(id, phase, actualDuration, baseDuration, startTime, commitTime) => ...}>` for programmatic timing.
actualDuration vs baseDuration: baseDuration is the cost with no memoization at all — their gap is what your memoization is buying.
Always profile a production build; dev builds are several times slower and StrictMode double-renders.
Throttle CPU 4× or 6× in Chrome Performance to model real devices before optimizing.
Distinguish the three costs: too many renders, one slow render, or slow commit (huge DOM mutation) — each has a different fix.
A component rendering 60× per second and taking 0.1ms is fine; one rendering twice and taking 200ms is the bug.
Rule: memoize the measured bottleneck, not the whole codebase — every memo is code you must keep correct forever.

chapters.title: Comparison Table & Trade-offs
points: memo — memoizes a COMPONENT; skips render when props shallow-equal; cost: prop comparison + retained tree.
useMemo — memoizes a VALUE; skips recomputation when deps equal; cost: closure + deps array + memory per instance.
useCallback — memoizes a FUNCTION reference; identical to useMemo(() => fn, deps); cost: same.
key — does not memoize anything; controls identity/matching, and can force a full remount.
useRef — persists a mutable value across renders and NEVER triggers a re-render; use for values the UI doesn't display.
useSyncExternalStore — subscribes to external state with a selector, so only actually-affected components render.

Which to reach for: child re-renders too much → memo + stable props; a computation is slow → useMemo; a function feeds a memo/effect → useCallback; a list reorders wrong → keys; a value shouldn't cause renders → ref.
Costs of memoization in general: memory retained, dep arrays that go stale, harder-to-read code, and comparison work on every render.
Memoization is all-or-nothing at a boundary — it only pays off if EVERY prop crossing it is stable.
React Compiler changes the calculus: it memoizes automatically and correctly, so hand-written memo is becoming a legacy/edge-case tool.
Order of preference: fix structure (colocate/split/children) → then memoize → then virtualize.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Gotchas
points: Wrapping a child in memo while passing an inline arrow/object/array prop — memo never hits; the comparison is pure overhead.
Using array index as key on a reorderable or filterable list — state and DOM attach to the wrong items.
Random keys — a full remount every render, losing focus, scroll, animation, and input state.
Provider value object created inline — re-renders every consumer on every provider render.
Lying to the deps array (omitting a dep to 'stop the loop') — creates stale closures reading old props/state.
Chasing 'zero re-renders' as a goal — re-renders are normal and usually cheap; only slow ones matter.
useMemo around a trivial expression (`useMemo(() => a + b, [a,b])`) — the hook costs more than the addition.
Assuming memo does a deep compare — `{a:1}` vs `{a:1}` are different references and fail shallow equality.
Mutating state in place (`arr.push(x); setArr(arr)`) — same reference, so React bails out and nothing updates.
Defining a component inside another component's body — a new type every render, so React unmounts and remounts the whole subtree, destroying its state.
Spreading unknown props (`{...props}`) into a memo'd child — one unstable field you never see kills the memo.
Custom memo comparators that compare too much (deep equal on a big object) — the comparison becomes the bottleneck.

chapters.title: Summary: The Decision Flow
points: Render = call the function; commit = touch the DOM. Most re-renders never touch the DOM.
Default behavior: a component re-renders when its own state changes, when its parent re-renders, or when its context value changes.
Reconciliation matches by (type, position), falling back to `key` among siblings — different type or different key means unmount + remount.
Keys are for identity, not for performance-tuning; stable data IDs, unique among siblings.
memo stops the parent-cascade; useMemo/useCallback exist mostly to keep the props crossing that memo boundary referentially stable.
Memoization only works as a complete chain — one unstable reference anywhere invalidates the whole thing.
Structural fixes (colocate state, split components, pass `children`) are free and beat memoization; try them first.
Profile in a production build with the DevTools Profiler before adding any memo — optimize the measured bottleneck only.
For huge lists, virtualize; for expensive non-urgent updates, useDeferredValue/startTransition; for non-visual values, useRef.
React Compiler automates most of this — write clean, pure, idiomatic components and let it memoize.
Checklist: Is it actually slow? → Can I move state down? → Can I pass children? → Then memo + stable props. → Then virtualize.
